endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: Organizations need to consider the benefits of these tools, as well as the risk of creating a surveillance environment that could affect the dignity and morale of employees and even create unsafe or counterproductive situations through evasions or workarounds by employees.

endorsements.title: Human-centered digital ecosystem: safeguarding healthcare workers' sleep, ergonomics, and occupational health
endorsements.quote: Governance should therefore distinguish between tools designed to reduce avoidable workload and systems designed to monitor employee behavior.

commentary.bottom_line: No study supplied tests whether evaluating workplace AI tools for surveillance risk protects employee dignity, morale, or trust, and no study documents the hazard itself. The recommendation rests on one framework (CHAI Responsible AI Guide) and one commentary, both phrased as expert judgment.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. Two endorsements, a framework and a commentary, support the recommendation through expert opinion only. Under GRADE conventions this yields no direct evidence, and certainty cannot be rated for any outcome, including morale, turnover, or employee trust.

The CHAI guide states that surveillance tools may prompt employee evasions or workarounds that create unsafe or counterproductive situations. That pathway would link workplace monitoring to patient harm, but no supplied study measures workaround frequency, their effect on care, or whether a pre-deployment review reduces them.

The commentary proposes that governance separate tools built to reduce avoidable workload from tools built to monitor employee behavior. This distinction may give review committees a usable sorting rule, although no study reports how reliably reviewers apply it or what the review costs in staff time.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare health systems or units that screen workplace AI tools for surveillance risk against those that do not, with measured outcomes such as staff-reported dignity and trust, burnout, turnover, documented workarounds, and downstream patient-safety events. Descriptive work documenting how often monitoring features appear in productivity and safety tools would also establish whether the hazard occurs at meaningful rates.
commentary.underserved_note: No study was supplied, so no test included staff at Medicaid-serving or safety-net facilities, workers with limited English proficiency, or workers with low literacy. Lower-wage and hourly health care workers, who may be more exposed to productivity monitoring, have no evidence describing either the hazard or the safeguard in their settings.
